items.title: Topic Seven Concludes: Wealth, Praise, and Friendship's Real Sources

items.zh: 謂如有一，昔餘生中作及增長施福業事；由此因緣，今生巨富大財寶家，乃至眾多府庫盈積。
items.en: It refers to one who, in some former life, performed and repeatedly cultivated meritorious acts of giving; by this cause, in this life, one is born into a family of vast wealth, its storehouses filled to overflowing.

items.zh: 謂如有一，不以假偽㪷秤函等，諂誑陵蔑妄言等事，而致財寶；但以如法作業伎能，依法不暴，而致財寶。彼既如是，眾咸唱言：賢哉儒士！乃能如法作業伎能引致財寶。
items.en: It refers to one who does not resort to false measures and scales, deceptive containers or letters, flattery, contempt, or falsehood to acquire wealth, but earns it only through lawful work and genuine skill, honestly and without violence. Such a person, everyone declares: what a worthy soul! — able to acquire wealth entirely through lawful labour and skill.

items.zh: 謂如有一，現前多有種種家產，遠離慳垢，不悋資具，以正安樂而自歡娛，乃至友朋、親戚、耆長。彼諸人等便相佐助，引致財寶，守護滋息。
items.en: It refers to one who, possessing considerable family wealth, remains free of the stain of stinginess, is never grudging with their resources, and takes wholesome joy in sharing it — with friends, relatives, and elders alike. Such people, in turn, gladly help them, bringing further wealth their way, protecting it, and making it grow.

items.zh: 復次，今當略辨上所說義。
謂略顯示恭敬、利養二種因緣。持戒擅名譽者，顯恭敬因緣；所餘諸句，顯利養因緣。謂因力故，士用力故，助伴力故。
items.en: This briefly reveals two kinds of cause: the cause of respect, and the cause of material gain. "Keeping precepts, one commands renown" reveals the cause of respect; the remaining lines reveal the causes of material gain — the power of karmic cause, the power of human effort, and the power of supportive companions.

items.title: Topic Eight Opens: The Spring That Never Stops Flowing

items.zh: 齊何泉止息？於何逕不通？世間諸苦樂，何處無餘滅？
items.en: At what point does the spring cease flowing? At what point does the path no longer run through? Where is the world's suffering and pleasure alike extinguished, without remainder?

items.zh: 若於是處所，眼耳及與鼻舌身意、名色，永滅盡無餘。齊此泉止息，於斯逕不通，世間諸苦樂，是處無餘滅。
items.en: Wherever eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind — together with mental and physical existence itself — are permanently and completely extinguished without remainder: precisely there does the spring cease flowing, precisely there does the path no longer run through, and precisely there is the world's suffering and pleasure alike extinguished without remainder.

items.zh: 云何為泉？謂六觸處。何以故？譬如泉池能生諸水，水所繫屬、堪任觸用；又能存養男女大小，下及禽獸，乃至一切未盡枯竭。
items.en: What is the spring? It refers to the six fields of contact. Why is this so? Just as a spring or pool constantly generates water, water belonging to and drawn from it, fit for use and contact — sustaining men and women, young and old, and even animals — so long as it has not yet run dry.

items.zh: 六內觸處亦復如是。一切愚夫六境界觸之所觸用；又能存養，乃至是中諸貪愛水未盡枯竭。
items.en: The six internal fields of contact are just the same: every foolish, unlearned being makes use of contact with the six kinds of objects, and is sustained by it, so long as the water of craving within has not yet run dry.

items.title: Topic Eight Concludes: A Graduated Map From Ordinary Being to Final Nirvāṇa

items.zh: 云何為逕？逕有二種。一、煩惱逕，二者、業逕。此中逕者，意明因義。
items.en: What is the path? The path has two kinds: first, the path of affliction; and second, the path of karma. Here, "path" means precisely "cause."

items.zh: 云何苦樂？謂或於現法六種觸處為緣所生，或安受，受所攝；或不安受，受所攝；或於後法煩惱攝持妙行、惡行為緣所生，或安受，受所攝；或不安受，受所攝。於何處所，如是六處及名色等無餘滅盡？謂無餘依涅槃界中。
若諸異生，泉逕苦樂一切無缺，亦未有捨。若諸有學，缺而未捨。若諸無學，逕及當來所有苦樂亦缺亦捨，不復現行；泉及現法所有苦樂亦缺亦捨，有餘依故，猶復現行。是故無餘涅槃界中，說彼一切無餘盡滅。
items.en: In ordinary beings, the spring, the path, and suffering-and-pleasure are all entirely present, without deficiency, and not yet abandoned. In trainees, they are deficient but not yet abandoned. In those beyond training, the path and all future suffering-and-pleasure are both deficient and abandoned, no longer manifesting; but the spring and the suffering-and-pleasure of the present life are both deficient and abandoned, yet still manifest, since a remainder of past conditions still remains. Therefore, it is said that within the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder, all of this is extinguished without exception, leaving nothing behind.

items.zh: 復次，今當略辨上所說義。謂略顯示於現法中因及苦樂，於後法中因及苦樂，於無餘依涅槃界中皆悉永滅。當知是名此中略義。

blocks.text: The rest of yesterday's answer, then a new question in the form of a riddle: where does the spring stop flowing? The answer is a short map of the whole path.

"Giving generously, one possesses wealth": giving in a former life, by the **power of cause**, brings birth into a rich family. Master Cháng Bǎi: regretting a gift after giving diminishes one's own merit; when the result comes, one cannot enjoy it.

"Speaking truthfully, one earns praise": one who earns wealth by lawful work and skill, without false measures or deception (Venerable Miào Jìng: 函 means both a container and a document): the **power of human effort**.
"Giving freely, one gathers friends": the wealthy person who shares with friends, relatives, and elders: the **power of supportive companions**.
The treatise sums up: precepts bring respect; the rest bring material gain. Venerable Miào Jìng: "renown through precepts" is chiefly a monastic matter; "praise through truthfulness" is a lay one.

"At what point does the spring cease flowing? … Wherever eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, together with name and form, are completely extinguished." Master Cháng Bǎi: only nirvāṇa without remainder is such a place.

The **spring** is the six fields of contact. Just as a spring constantly yields water, the six senses constantly yield contact, and beings live on it, "so long as the water of craving within has not yet run dry". Venerable Miào Jìng: the craving they produce is the water.

subs.head: Two paths, three kinds of people

blocks.text: The **path** is twofold: of affliction and of karma; "path" means "cause". Master Cháng Bǎi: affliction is the road that leads to karma.

In ordinary beings the spring, the path, and pleasure-and-pain are all present and not abandoned. In trainees they are reduced but not abandoned. In those beyond training they are abandoned, yet the spring and present feeling still appear "because of the remainder" (the body). Master Cháng Bǎi: there is only bodily feeling, no mental suffering. At death, all ceases.

quiz.q: What does the treatise give as the cause of "giving generously, one possesses wealth"?
options: meritorious giving performed and increased in a former life, so one is born into a family of vast wealth now
quiz.why: "It refers to one who, in some former life, performed and repeatedly cultivated meritorious acts of giving; by this cause, in this life, one is born into a family of vast wealth." Master Cháng Bǎi: this is the power of cause — seeds planted in past lives.

quiz.q: What does Master Cháng Bǎi say "increased" in "performed and increased meritorious giving" implies?
options: not regretting the gift; regret diminishes the merit, so the result cannot be enjoyed or brings no joy
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: if after giving one regrets it, one is diminishing one's own merit; when the result comes, one cannot enjoy it, or enjoys it without gladness.

quiz.q: In its brief explanation, which two kinds of cause and three powers does the treatise say the four lines reveal?
options: renown through precepts is the cause of respect; the other three are causes of material gain — the power of cause, of human effort, and of companions
all four are causes of respect
all four are the power of cause
quiz.why: "'Keeping precepts, one commands renown' reveals the cause of respect; the remaining lines reveal the causes of material gain — the power of karmic cause, the power of human effort, and the power of supportive companions." Master Cháng Bǎi: giving bringing wealth is the power of cause; truthfulness bringing praise is the power of human effort.

quiz.q: What does Master Cháng Bǎi say is the place "completely extinguished without remainder" in the answer verse?
options: nirvāṇa without remainder — only there do spring, path, and suffering-and-pleasure all end
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: only nirvāṇa without remainder can be where the spring ceases, the path no longer runs, and the world's suffering and pleasure are extinguished without remainder.

quiz.q: In the spring simile, what does the "water" stand for, per the two masters?
options: craving — when the six faculties meet lovely objects, craving arises like water from a spring
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: the six fields of contact are a spring; the craving they produce is the water flowing out — the water stands for the affliction of craving. Master Cháng Bǎi: when the six faculties meet objects, craving arises, just as a spring produces water.

quiz.q: What two kinds of "path" does the treatise name, and what does "path" mean?
options: the path of affliction and of karma — "path" here means cause
quiz.why: "The path has two kinds: first, the path of affliction; and second, the path of karma. Here, 'path' means precisely 'cause.'" Master Cháng Bǎi: affliction is a road that leads to karma.

quiz.q: For those beyond training, the treatise says the spring and present suffering-and-pleasure are "both deficient and abandoned... yet still manifest." How do the English and the lecture differ?
options: the English has "deficient yet still manifest," dropping "abandoned"; Cháng Bǎi says the arhat has only bodily feeling, no mental feeling, abiding always in supreme equanimity
the lecture says arhats still have afflictions
quiz.why: The treatise says the spring and present suffering-and-pleasure are "both deficient and abandoned, yet still manifest because of the remainder." The English omits "abandoned." Master Cháng Bǎi: there is only bodily feeling, no mental feeling; the mind abides always in supreme equanimity and no affliction arises from circumstances.
